text: In right-angled triangles,  the square on the side subtending the right-angle is equal to the (sum of the) squares on the sides containing the right-angle.  Let $ABC$ be a right-angled triangle having the angle $BAC$a right-angle. I say that the square on $BC$ is equal to the (sum of the) squares on $BA$ and $AC$.
For let the square $BDEC$ have been described on $BC$, and (the squares) $GB$ and $HC$ on $AB$ and $AC$ (respectively) [Prop.~1.46].
And let $AL$ have been drawn through point $A$ parallel to either of $BD$ or $CE$ [Prop.~1.31].
And let $AD$ and $FC$ have been joined.

And since angles $BAC$ and $BAG$ are each right-angles, then two straight-lines $AC$ and $AG$, not lying on the same side, make the adjacent angles with some straight-line $BA$, at the point $A$ on it, (whose sum is) equal to two right-angles.
assertion: AC and AG make adjacent angles with BA (whose sum is) equal to two right-angles

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: two straight-lines $AC$ and $AG$, not lying on the same side, make the adjacent angles with some straight-line $BA$, at the point $A$ on it, (whose sum is) equal to two right-angles

text: Thus, $CA$ is straight-on to $AG$ [Prop.~1.14].
So, for the same (reasons), $BA$ is also straight-on to $AH$.
And since angle $DBC$ is equal to $FBA$, for (they are) both right-angles, let $ABC$ have been added to both.
assertion: angle DBC is equal to angle FBA (both being right-angles)

spans.label: glue
spans.text: , let $ABC$ have been added to both.

text: Thus, the whole (angle) $DBA$ is equal to the whole (angle) $FBC$.
assertion: whole angle DBA is equal to whole angle FBC

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the whole (angle) $DBA$ is equal to the whole (angle) $FBC$

text: And since $DB$ is equal to $BC$, and $FB$ to $BA$, the two (straight-lines) $DB$, $BA$ are equal to the two (straight-lines) $CB$, $BF$, respectively.
assertion: the two DB, BA are equal to the two CB, BF respectively

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the two (straight-lines) $DB$, $BA$ are equal to the two (straight-lines) $CB$, $BF$, respectively

text: And angle $DBA$ (is) equal to angle $FBC$.
assertion: angle DBA is equal to angle FBC

text: Thus, the base $AD$ [is] equal to the base $FC$,
assertion: base AD is equal to base FC

text: and the triangle $ABD$ is equal to the triangle $FBC$ [Prop.~1.4].
assertion: triangle ABD is equal to triangle FBC

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: triangle $ABD$ is equal to the triangle $FBC$

text: And  parallelogram $BL$ [is] double (the area) of triangle $ABD$. For they have the same base, $BD$, and are between the same parallels, $BD$ and $AL$  [Prop.~1.41].
assertion: parallelogram BL is double the area of triangle ABD

spans.label: assumption
spans.text: they have the same base, $BD$, and are between the same parallels, $BD$ and $AL$

text: And  square $GB$ is double (the area) of triangle $FBC$. For again they have the same base, $FB$, and are between the same parallels, $FB$ and $GC$ [Prop.~1.41].
assertion: square GB is double the area of triangle FBC

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: square $GB$ is double (the area) of triangle $FBC$

spans.label: assumption
spans.text: they have the same base, $FB$, and are between the same parallels, $FB$ and $GC$

text: [And the doubles of equal things are equal to one another.]
assertion: the doubles of equal things are equal to one another

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the doubles of equal things are equal to one another

text: Thus, the parallelogram $BL$ is also equal to the square $GB$.
assertion: parallelogram BL is equal to square GB

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the parallelogram $BL$ is also equal to the square $GB$

text: So, similarly, $AE$ and $BK$ being joined,  the parallelogram $CL$ can be shown (to be)  equal to the square $HC$.
assertion: parallelogram CL is equal to square HC

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the parallelogram $CL$ can be shown (to be)  equal to the square $HC$

text: Thus, the whole square $BDEC$ is equal to the (sum of the) two squares $GB$ and $HC$.
assertion: whole square BDEC is equal to the sum of the two squares GB and HC

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the whole square $BDEC$ is equal to the (sum of the) two squares $GB$ and $HC$

text: And the square $BDEC$ is described on $BC$,
assertion: square BDEC is described on BC

text: and the (squares) $GB$ and $HC$ on $BA$ and $AC$ (respectively).
assertion: squares GB and HC are described on BA and AC respectively

text: Thus, the square on the side $BC$ is equal to the (sum of the) squares on the sides $BA$ and $AC$.
assertion: square on side BC is equal to the sum of the squares on sides BA and AC

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: square on the side $BC$ is equal to the (sum of the) squares on the sides $BA$ and $AC$

text: Thus, in right-angled triangles,  the square on the side subtending the right-angle is equal to the (sum of the) squares on the sides surrounding the right-[angle]. (Which is) the very thing it was required to show.
